We convinced the board to hedge. Then the currency went the other way.
The right decision cost us more than two years.
A financial institution I was advising had borrowed in dollars to fund its local currency lending. A textbook mismatch, and one the board understood.
We took them through the options and recommended hedging the exposure. Best practice, we said, and we meant it. They accepted.
Everyone in that room, myself included, expected the local currency to weaken. It had been weakening for years.
It strengthened instead.
That alone would have been survivable. The structure of the deal was the real problem. The variation margin terms in the hedge were set against us, so every move in the currency pulled cash out of the institution. As soon as the local currency began to appreciate, the margin calls started, and they kept coming.
Two years later the position closed. We had told the board that hedging would take the currency question off the table. It did. It never occurred to us to tell them it would not take the cash question off the table, because we had not thought hard enough about the terms we had signed.
Then the next facility came up.
Getting the board back to a hedge was very difficult. They had seen what best practice cost them, in cash, every month, for two years. They no longer believed in hedging!
Therefore, we did not go back and renegotiate the margin and collateral terms. We left the exposure open.
Global economic conditions turned inside the period. The perennial flight to safety occurred, and the local currency was battered. The institution sat with a dollar liability against a local currency book, unhedged, and took a heavy foreign exchange loss. Far heavier than the hedge had ever cost.
Two lessons, and the second is the expensive one.
Unless you are in the business of buying and selling hedges, being on one side of a currency exposure means you hedge it. The negotiation is about the terms, not about whether.
And a bad outcome is not proof of a bad decision. We had made the right call, priced it badly, and then let the price talk us out of the call itself.
I now spend more time on the margin and collateral terms of a hedge than on the decision to hedge. The decision is usually the easy part. The terms are where the money is.
